Some of the young Jewish fighters, including young Bundists like Marek Edelman, were able to escape through the sewers from the flaming shell of the ghetto, and they fought until the end of the war as partisans. But I want to say something else about the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, which is that a year later, the Red Army had defeated the Nazis at Stalingrad and had rolled through Ukraine. It had liberated Auschwitz. It had gone into Poland, and it had gotten all the way to Praga, which is a Warsaw suburb just on the other side of the Vistula River. And when it was there, it released radio broadcasts calling on the Polish population to rebel against the Nazis, and the Home Army did. The Home Army heeded the call, and it launched a giant citywide rebellion in Warsaw. After that rebellion kicked off, the Red Army did not go to Warsaw to save those fighters. It waited on the other side of the river, and it watched. The reason it did that was that Stalin did not like the Polish Home Army, and he was quite happy for it and the Nazis to kill each other off and save him the trouble. So the Red Army watched while the Nazis brought in reinforcements to liquidate the Warsaw city rebellion, and while they burned Warsaw, the Paris of the East, and bulldozed it block by block. Then after Warsaw was destroyed and its entire civilian population was rounded into transit camps, the Red Army rolled in to take the wreckage. “They Have to Refuse” Daniel Denvir What, then, is the significance — historically and morally — of this uprising that was doomed to fail? Molly Crabapple I think the significance of it is that it was the most defiant act of the human spirit possible: people who knew that there was no chance of survival and so demanded to set the terms for their own death. But I think there’s something else about it too. It’s not just about the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising; it’s also about what it meant that the Home Army did not support it, and what it meant that it made that sort of brutal calculus. By the time one is thinking like that, it’s almost become too late. At so many moments, different choices could have been made. The French and the British could have upheld their treaty obligations and fought back against Germany when it decided to invade Poland. That’s one thing. The Polish population at large could have resisted the ghettoization of Jews, as opposed to largely going along with it and sometimes cheering it on. The Polish Home Army could have brutally punished the blackmailing industry from the start, the way that it punished people who snitched out Polish Home Army soldiers. The Polish Home Army could have given Jews in the ghetto guns before 90 percent of them had been murdered. At every single moment, there was a chance for different choices to have been made, even though at each moment those choices became more and more constricted. But for me, the lesson of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising is that people cannot let it get to that, and they have to refuse. They have to refuse to allow their neighbors to be taken, to be thrown in jail and concentration camps, to be shut off from them. When I look at Minneapolis, where so many white American citizens risked their lives to get out into the streets and physically, with their cars and with their bodies, prevent their neighbors from being taken to concentration camps — and two white American citizens were shot in the head doing this — that’s, I think, what is needed. It’s that refusal from the start, before it’s at the point where all you have is young people committing an impossibly valiant act of mass suicide. Anyone who looks at places that have suffered under the boot of unrelenting violence and oppression knows that it didn’t turn all the people in those places into saints and prophets. Did the Nazis Settle the Argument? Daniel Denvir Perhaps the most profound contradiction that your book surfaces for me is that while the Bund was clearly morally in the right, it’s the Zionists who can argue, in a sense, that they were historically right about Europe: that there where they lived, in Poland, was, it turned out, not their home; that Jews were surrounded by people who would, in many cases, help the Nazis murder 90 percent of them. How do you untangle this twisted way in which the Nazis settled the debate in the Zionists’ favor? Molly Crabapple There are two things. The fact that the Jews of Poland were murdered and that the Jews of the Yishuv, the Jewish community in Palestine, were not does not come down to anything more than historical contingency. The reason the Jews in Palestine were not all murdered by the Nazis was that it was a British colony, and the British — not the Jews, the British — were able to stop the Nazi General Erwin Rommel at El-Alamein in Egypt. And if the Nazis had been able to take Palestine, which they wanted to, they would have murdered every single Jew there, and there was no plan to prevent that. Perhaps people with the condescension of history would later look at that and think how stupid it was to concentrate an entire community that was the target of genocide so close to Europe, in one little place. To me, it’s contingency, and I don’t believe in making your political and life philosophy based on something so utterly contingent. In terms of whether Poland, Ukraine, and Lithuania were so racist that there was nothing you could have done — that these were just incomprehensibly racist places. . . . and ok, there were good people there, there were comrades; no group is entirely one way or the other. Ninety percent of Polish Jews were murdered, but that meant that about three hundred thousand Polish Jews survived, which was the largest community of survivors in Europe of any country. Within a few years, most of those will have fled the country because of the grinding racism that still remained and the murders — which sometimes were about the conflation of Jews and Communists, but sometimes were just murders of Jews who went back to their house and found that someone else was living in it. It would be extremely hard for me to look at that and say, “Wow, people who left were dumb.” I think it’s amazing that people like Marek Edelman, the great Bundist, did stay. He stayed his entire life; he took part in the Solidarność movement that overthrew the Communist dictatorship. He died in Poland in 2009, and the Bund’s anthem was sung over his coffin. Edelman was not permitted to speak because he was not a Zionist. An honor to his memory. It was that combination of the political repression of living under a Stalinist dictatorship, the constant racist murders, and the horror of living in a place that was essentially a graveyard for the Jewish people of Europe. The thing I want to add to complicate it is that it’s very hard for people to know. There have been many minorities — I think about black Americans — who have been subjected to the most foul and murderous and evil types of violence again and again and again and yet still have fought not to colonize Liberia, but to have decent, dignified, free, liberated, and equal lives in the land where they were born and the land that they helped build. I don’t think anyone could look at them and say that they were naive or that they were wrong or that they were doing anything but engaging in the basic human right and duty to insist that here where you live is your country. And the shame, for me, is on Europe. It’s not on Jews who thought that they could fight to make Europe better. What sort of archives informed your research, and how did those archives survive? And how did you convert these incomplete, and sometimes nonexistent or destroyed, archives into these fuller stories? Molly Crabapple First of all, I’m not an academic. I didn’t even go to academic college. I never wrote a term paper. I don’t come from this world, and so I had no desire to put on the drag of an academic and pretend to be something that I’m not. I’m an artist and a writer. I also believe that history is everyone’s birthright, and I know that the vast majority of people do not read academic books. They’re not interested in reading them. They find that the prose style makes their eyes go blank. So, when I was writing this book, I was like, “How can I write this in a way that my tattoo artist friend will read it? How do I write this so my burlesque dancer friend will read it? How do I write this so that people who think history books aren’t for them will read it?” I always thought about that. I was like, how do I make this something that will be worth the while of people who don’t usually read history? There were a few choices that I made. The first was that I would do a character-driven book, because people relate better to the stories of individuals than they do to big theoretical tomes. I’m not saying that big theoretical tomes aren’t important; I’m just saying that they will never have a mass audience. I’m just like, I’m going to do something personality-driven. The second decision I made was that if I was going to embark on this, I would follow the things that interested me. And I hate conferences; I hate leftist meetings. I am a DSA member who avoids them at every moment. I also think that often the real things that happen, the real dynamics, are not the official decisions of the meeting but rather the things that happen behind the scenes. So, I’m like, I’m not going to write this book and make it just a list of sh-t that was decided at conferences, because I don’t think it’s real, and I also don’t think it’s interesting. I was like, what am I interested in? I’m interested in friendship, sex, danger, love, people being ridiculous, betrayal, internationalism. I’m interested in the physical world. I am someone who thinks that so much of the fabric of being in a movement is waiting outside a jail cell to give someone cigarettes after they’re out, or marching in the cold when your feet are really cold and the wet is getting through the soles of your shoes, but you’re holding your friend’s hand. It’s staying up really late to hand-paint banners. It’s a very physical thing to be in a movement. It’s not just a head thing. So, I was very concerned with this book being something that was set in the physical world. My father said it was one of the only books he’d read about revolutionaries where they had bodies. The other thing I will say is that I went into this with a huge sense of inferiority. And because I felt this huge sense of inferiority, I was like, I have to know everything. I cannot just read the Bund archives and the academic books. I have to read what their enemies said. I have to read what the Bolsheviks said. I have to read every book about the history of Poland. I have to know what tangos they were listening to in 1930. I have to know what people would eat for breakfast. I have to know how people dressed. I have to know the type of chair they sat on. I want to know what the Siege of Warsaw looked like. What did peasants do with their cows, and were they selling the milk? They were. I wanted to know everything. So I did an amount of research that was psychopathic and lunatic. I wrote a thousand-page book at first — or a thousand-page mess, I should say, not book — and then cut that thousand-page mess into the 380-page book we have now, excluding many, things. Now, in terms of the research I did, I learned to read Yiddish. I studied for two years at this amazing summer program at the YIVO Institute for Jewish Research. It’s a twenty-hour-a-week, six-week, beat-Yiddish-into-your-donkey-brain type of program. I read all of the Yiddish Bundist canon, like Di Geshikhte fun Bund and Doyres Bundistn . These are big biographical dictionaries, so boring, and the official history, the worst-written official history in all of official histories. I read all these memoirs. I was also very concerned with women, because the Bund had a lot of women in leadership, but for some reason a lot of the women’s memoirs didn’t end up getting translated into English. So, you get the impression that it’s a much more male movement than it is. Even if you read the biographical dictionary, which is filled with women — filled to the brim with women, women who are physicians and fighters and orators and theorists. Also, because I decided this book was going to be character-driven, I largely chose who my main characters would be based on who had good memoirs, because I wanted to have a sense of people’s interiority. It’s very hard to get a sense of someone’s interiority if all they left you is economics texts that they wrote. That’s one of the reasons that Sofia Dubnova — who was a Bundist, a poet, and a sex columnist, and the wife of the Bund’s leader in Poland — one of the reasons I really focus on her is that she wrote an amazing memoir called Bread and Matzah that gave you such a view of what kind of woman she was, what kind of mother, what kind of artist. It was the same with Vladimir Medem, one of the Bund’s theorists. He wrote an amazing memoir, and then his wife wrote a bitchy memoir too that sort of supplements his and fills in some holes in it. Because I wanted to write inside people’s heads, I had to read what they said was inside their heads. I read lots of stuff by Russian writers, like the Nikolai Sukhanov book about the day-to-day of the February Revolution, and Kerensky’s pompous and self-justifying memoirs. I read stuff by Bundists who became Bolsheviks, like Moisei Rafes. I read stuff by Zionists. I read the Zionist press denouncing the Bund. And then I read biographies of Zionists, like Tom Segev’s biography of David Ben-Gurion, A State at Any Cost . That was the book that gave me the anecdote about Ben-Gurion in the synagogue losing an argument and then threatening to shoot the Bundists down like dogs. Segev was the one who surfaced that one, not me. In terms of the archives, a lot of it was looking for stuff about Volkovysk, my great-grandfather’s hometown. Also, there are these things called Yizkor books. These are crucial for anyone doing this type of research. They’re combination oral history and amateur sociology books that were compiled after the Holocaust about pretty much every town in Eastern Europe. They’re amazing, because they’re just people’s memories of this town. Many of the most vivid passages in my book, like the part where there’s a fight on Yom Kippur in front of the synagogue, are from the Yizkor book. I find them to be the richest, most amazing resource. I always tell Jewish people who are trying to do family history that if they know the hometown their family came from — if their family came from a town in Eastern Europe, and they know what it is — look at the Yizkor book. That’s where you want to go. I also looked at a lot of regular press archives. If you ever want to think about the degradation of print media, know that in 1905, the Brooklyn Daily Eagle had a correspondent in Łódź reporting on the revolution on the ground. So many of the most vivid things I got were from the Associated Press wire, or The New York Times , or the Herald Tribune . The part when all of these revolutionaries in Siberia who’ve just been freed by the new government are racing to get home to beat the frost, and one of the guys is still in his leg irons because the blacksmiths are all on strike — that’s from the Associated Press. That was from an interview that guy did with AP, who were trying to get to Siberia to interview these political exiles. I also looked at the black press a lot. The New York Age is an amazing resource, and it’s all digitized. I don’t understand how you have this press archive that’s all digitized, all text-searchable, in English, and it’s not constantly being referred to for what the black press thought of things. It really enriched my history, being able to not just quote the Times , but to quote the Age . What did they think about the pogroms? What did they think about revolution in Russia? I also I tried hard to look at photographic archives. For the Siege of Warsaw, for instance, there was this American photojournalist who was in Warsaw when the Nazi invasion started, and I think he was one of the last foreign journalists to be evacuated, and there’s a photo book of his photos from Warsaw, showing daily life under the siege. There’s a march I talk about that Sofia Dubnova is on in May 1917. She described it in her memoir, but I also looked at other descriptions of the march, and then I found there was silent video footage of the march, which is amazing. Then I would really try to look into the world that people were part of. Because ok, you’re a revolutionary, but you’re also someone who’s listening to music, and going to the movies, and wearing clothing. You’re part of your society. I got really into Polish tango, for instance, because it’s so cool — Polish interwar tango, a lot of which was released on a Jewish-owned record label called Syrena Rekord. I found out that one year the hit song was called “Suicide Tango,” by Mieczysław Fogg. And I was like, “This is so cool.” I was imagining someone listening to “Suicide Tango” on the gramophone during this actual incident where Bernard Goldstein and Polish socialists smash up a Polish nationalist restaurant. I was like, “What would have been playing? Imagine if it was this song,” because it was the year’s hit song. Modernity’s Double Edge Daniel Denvir It’s striking, reading the book, that it was the very same modernity that allowed Bundists and their socialist and communist comrades — and rivals, and enemies — to imagine a world of universal brotherhood, equality, and peace. It was that same modernity that facilitated racist, industrial, fascist mass murder on a scale theretofore unimaginable. If the Bund was premised on an excessively optimistic vision of modernity, have we perhaps now, in the wake of the Holocaust and so many other twentieth-century horrors, reverted to an excessively pessimistic understanding of modernity and of what sort of future might lie ahead? Molly Crabapple I don’t know. When I look at what sort of future might lie ahead, as imagined by our Silicon Valley tech lords, all they’re promising us is dystopia. A healthy skepticism of the idea of universal progress is probably good, because I think buying into the idea that technology and progress are always good is what enables people to be such suckers for the promises of fascist Silicon Valley dweebs. But it is also true that there are things about modernity that are . . . almost every week I think about how lucky I am to be a woman born at this time. I think about how even in my mother’s generation, she couldn’t get a mortgage. In my grandmother’s generation, her husband didn’t let her drive a car. All of these huge things that at every level you just had to overcome if you were a woman. Obviously, I’m fully cognizant of sexism. But by the same token, if I wanted to, I could drive a car, and a man does not have to give me permission. I’m allowed to get a credit card. I’m allowed to travel abroad. I am able to have control over reproduction, even though obviously the government’s desperate to take that away — but nonetheless, it’s still the truth. It’s funny — I have gotten into some arguments about this with some of my radical male friends who have told me, “Nothing is better for women.” And I’m like, “No, it is. Truly.” The Jewish Left in America, Then and Now Daniel Denvir Zooming back to look at this century-plus of US Jewish history, these émigrés and exiles contributed to the foundation of the twentieth-century labor movement, with all of its drama, promise, and failure. But an explicitly socialist — let alone non-Zionist or even anti-Zionist — Jewish left receded very dramatically throughout the latter half of the twentieth century. Many parents and grandparents of today’s younger anti-Zionist socialist Jews became liberal Zionists and loyal liberal Democrats. How would you trace the arc of the Jewish American left from the early twentieth-century Lower East Side to today, and where does the revival of a youthful, socialist, anti-Zionist Jewish American left fit into that arc, and what does it tell us about what might lie ahead? Molly Crabapple There are a few fundamental things that really were blows to the postwar Jewish left. The first is McCarthyism. The Left in America did not merely fizzle; it was brutally crushed. The International Workers Order, which was an amazing, huge Jewish leftist group, a sort of Communist-linked organization, was liquidated by the government. Even some Bundist survivors — I asked their kids, “Why didn’t your parents do anything politically after the war? Your parents were so politically active in Poland.” And in addition to all of the reasons you would imagine, like that they were impoverished and psychologically destroyed refugees learning a new language and a new trade — one reason is that they were afraid of being deported as communists. We cannot overestimate the damage that McCarthyism did to the Jewish left. And when you look at the types of people who were called before the House Un-American Activities Committee, it will not shock you that they’re disproportionately Jewish. Another thing is that America has never been antisemitic in the way that Europe was. This doesn’t mean there wasn’t bigotry. It doesn’t mean there weren’t quotas and racism. But America’s fundamental structural racism is anti-blackness and anti-indigenous racism. And all the other forms of racism are largely dependent on geopolitics, in my opinion, and are malleable. But it’s not a place that is built on hating Jews because of the false accusation that they killed Jesus, the way Catholic Europe was. Because of that, there were so many opportunities: people had the chance to go to college, enter the middle class, move to the suburbs. Most people don’t want to be factory workers, and they don’t want their kids to be factory workers. Being a factory worker is really hard. If they’re a factory worker in a garment sweatshop and they have the chance for their kid to become a college professor, they would rather their kid became a college professor. In general, people would largely prefer to do less backbreaking and higher-paid work rather than extremely low-paid work that also destroys your body. And America gave Jews an opportunity to do that in a way that, by and large, they did not have in Poland. Obviously, Zionism and the hegemony of Zionism, especially after 1967. I think the movie Exodus is responsible for warping so many boomer minds. Also, every immigrant group in America loses its language. The grandchildren and great-grandchildren of Italian immigrants today, by and large, don’t speak Italian. The great-grandchildren of the Irish immigrants of yesteryear, by and large, don’t speak Gaelic. Some do, but by and large they don’t. America is just this machine for stripping people of their language and culture, especially during the years when such a premium was placed on assimilation. Even though the Bund tried very hard to inoculate Yiddish into its children, it was no match for America as an imperial project. By and large, the descendants of the Eastern European Jewish immigrants who were socialists or communists or anarchists, or just plain old sweatshop workers, in 1903 — by and large, their boomer and Gen X descendants became liberal Democrats. Another reason was also Franklin D. Roosevelt and the New Deal and the amazing amount of loyalty they generated. That peeled a lot of people away from the Socialist Party. But in general, the descendants of the Jewish radicals of 1903, by 1970, were probably in the majority middle-class liberal Democrats with jobs in the professions. But we’re also going through a moment where the old liberal-Democrat, secure-a-job-in-the-professions lifestyle is being destroyed — and not just for Jews, for everyone. And while the grandchildren of the Bundist sweatshop workers might have become the Democratic-voting doctors living in the suburbs, their grandchildren are quite likely to be the downwardly mobile adjunct getting paid $12,000 a year and sharing an overpriced apartment with three other people despite the fact that they’re in their thirties. I think the same trajectory that’s leading so many precarious young people to socialism is having the same effect on Jews as on everyone else.
